hook_text: Engineers said the railway would take five years. The army said: one year. The difference was paid in lives.
clip_script: Thailand, 1943. In the jungle, thin men swing picks at solid rock. They are prisoners of war: British, Australian, Dutch, American. Beside them are far more workers from across Asia, forced or tricked into labour. Japan needs a railway to Burma, 415 kilometres long, and it needs it fast. Food is a handful of rice. Then the monsoon comes, and cholera with it. At a cutting called Hellfire Pass, men work through the night by firelight. By the time the line is finished, about 12 000 prisoners and up to 100 000 Asian labourers are dead. Why so brutal? Soldiers taught that surrender was shameful. Rules for prisoners ignored. Deadlines that ignored human limits. After the war, the guilty were tried. One South African survivor, Laurens van der Post, said he chose not to hate, because hatred keeps cruelty alive.
visual_style: A jungle ridge with a railway line being cut through rock; flickering torchlight in a deep cutting; a map line from Thailand to Burma; a ration bowl with a few grains of rice; a war cemetery with neat rows of headstones.
pacing: Slow, with a steady rhythm like hammer blows, easing at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to understand what prisoners endured and how the world responded.
